title: How the 2026 Browns Defense Plans to SURVIVE Without Myles Garrett
thumb_prompt: A football helmet with number ninety-five lying empty on the sideline grass at dusk, with shadows of new defensive players standing tall in the background, dramatic orange and brown lighting creating a sense of transition and determination.
thumb_subject: A determined young defensive end in a white and orange number fifty-seven jersey with his sleeves rolled up, facing the camera in a three-point stance

sections.heading: The Identity That Left on June Second

paragraphs.text: June second, twenty twenty-six. That is the day the Cleveland Browns traded Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams. Two-time Defensive Player of the Year. Future Hall of Famer. The man who wore number ninety-five for nine seasons. Gone. In return, the Browns received Jared Verse, a two-time Pro Bowl edge rusher, plus a twenty twenty-seven first-rounder, a twenty twenty-eight second-rounder, and a twenty twenty-nine third. But no matter how you spin the compensation, this is the first training camp since two thousand seventeen without Myles Garrett anchoring the defense. And here is what everyone is asking. Can this defense survive?

Let me be clear about something. Myles Garrett was not just a great player. He was a gravitational force. When Garrett lined up, offensive coordinators had to account for him on every single snap. Double teams. Triple teams. Slide protection his direction. He dictated how offenses attacked this defense. And when you lose that, you do not just lose sacks. You lose the entire ecosystem that player creates. Defensive tackle Maliek Collins got cleaner one-on-ones because Garrett commanded attention. Linebacker Carson Schwesinger could blitz from the edge knowing Garrett occupied two blockers. The secondary had extra milliseconds in coverage because quarterbacks felt pressure even when it was not there. That is what generational pass rushers do.

Here is the uncomfortable truth. ESPN reported the Browns ranked number four in yards allowed last season and number three in pass defense. They were also number five in defensive EPA per play. But here is the catch. How much of that was Myles Garrett? We are about to find out. Training camp is underway right now in Berea, and defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg is installing what Grant Delpit called an exotic scheme with a lot of disguise. Rutenberg kept the foundation of Jim Schwartz's attacking philosophy, but he is adding layers of deception. That makes sense. When you lose the best pure pass rusher in football, you need to manufacture pressure through scheme, not just raw talent.
card_lines: 2025: No. 4 yards allowed, No. 3 pass D

paragraphs.text: And this is where Jared Verse enters the story. Verse is twenty-four years old. He recorded twelve sacks, one hundred twenty-four tackles, and five forced fumbles in his first two NFL seasons with the Rams. He is a violent, mean, physical player. His own words. He told reporters his style is very violent, very mean, asking why do you think you can block me. That is the mentality. But here is what he is not. He is not Myles Garrett. Garrett had elite agility, a full repertoire of pass-rush moves, hands that could defeat any block. Verse is a power rusher who uses violence and physicality. That is a different style. And that means his teammates need to adjust how they play off him.

Now let us talk about the guys who have to step up. Isaiah McGuire. Fourth-round pick in twenty twenty-three out of Missouri. He is entering a contract year, and sources say he has been one of the standouts of training camp so far. McGuire recorded five and a half sacks and seventy-two tackles through his first three seasons. Not spectacular. But now, with Garrett gone, he has a golden opportunity to prove he can be a starting-caliber edge rusher in this league. Alex Wright is on the other side. He has been with the team since twenty twenty-two, and veteran defensive end Alex Wright told ninety-two point three The Fan that this defense has a chip on our shoulder. He said we were top three in sacks last season, and there were other people producing besides Myles.
card_lines: Isaiah McGuire: Contract year, camp standout
Top 3 in sacks wasn't just Garrett

paragraphs.text: Wright has a point. But he is also glossing over reality. Yes, the Browns had a deep pass rush rotation last year. But Myles Garrett set the NFL single-season sack record with twenty-three in twenty twenty-five. He was Defensive Player of the Year for the second time. That production does not just appear from thin air. Someone has to generate it. And if Verse, McGuire, and Wright cannot collectively replace even seventy percent of what Garrett did, this defense is in trouble. Because the rest of the AFC North is not getting easier. The Ravens still have Lamar Jackson. The Bengals still have Joe Burrow. The Steelers added Aaron Rodgers. This division is a gauntlet, and the Browns just lost their best weapon.

sections.heading: The Historic Precedent: Cleveland Defense at a Crossroads

paragraphs.text: Let me take you back in time. Because this is not the first time the Browns have had to reinvent their defensive identity. In the nineteen fifties, the Browns had Len Ford, a dominant defensive end who was the centerpiece of Paul Brown's championship defenses. Ford was so disruptive that teams literally invented the four-three defense to counter him. He won five All-NFL honors and recovered twenty fumbles, an NFL record at the time. That was the foundation of a dynasty. Then, in the nineteen eighties, Cleveland built another fearsome defense. Frank Minnifield and Hanford Dixon created the Dawg Pound identity. Carl Hairston brought Super Bowl experience from Philadelphia. Clay Matthews anchored the linebacker corps. That defense carried the Browns to five straight playoff appearances from nineteen eighty-five to nineteen eighty-nine.

But here is the common thread. Every great Browns defense was built on toughness, physicality, and a blue-collar identity. Cleveland has never been a finesse team. When they have won, it has been with a punishing ground game and a defense that leaves opposing teams longing for a return home. That is a direct quote from a historical analysis of this franchise. And right now, in August of twenty twenty-six, that identity is being tested. Can Todd Monken and Mike Rutenberg recapture that blue-collar defensive ethos without the best individual talent? Can they build a unit that is greater than the sum of its parts? Because that is what it will take. Garrett was a singular talent. The defense moving forward has to be a collective force.
card_lines: Browns identity: toughness, physicality, ground & pound

paragraphs.text: And here is where training camp becomes so critical. Camp is where identity is forged. It is where young players like Isaiah McGuire prove they belong. It is where veterans like Denzel Ward and Grant Delpit set the tone. Speaking of those two, the Browns just locked them both up to extensions. Ward got a two-year, sixty-two point two million dollar deal. Delpit signed a three-year, forty-eight million dollar extension. That is a massive financial commitment to the secondary. And it tells you where the Browns think this defense will win in twenty twenty-six. If they cannot dominate with pass rush, they will suffocate with coverage. Force quarterbacks to hold the ball. Create turnovers. Make offenses earn every single yard.
card_lines: Win with coverage, not just pass rush

paragraphs.text: Denzel Ward is entering his ninth season. He was the fourth overall pick in twenty eighteen, a two-time Pro Bowler, and one of the best man-coverage corners in the NFL. Tyson Campbell, acquired in a trade with Jacksonville for Greg Newsome, is the other starting corner. Grant Delpit is a ball-hawking safety who had three interceptions in the first week of camp alone. Ronnie Hickman is the other starting safety, and he has become one of the more underrated players in the league. ESPN's Daniel Oyefusi said this secondary is one of the best in the NFL. If that holds true, this defense can still be elite. But it will be a different kind of elite. Less about one man wrecking the game. More about eleven guys flying to the football.
card_lines: Ward: 9th year, 2x Pro Bowl, elite man coverage
Delpit: 3 INTs in first camp week
Hickman underrated, Oyefusi says top NFL unit

paragraphs.text: Carson Schwesinger is another key piece. Reigning Defensive Rookie of the Year. He is entering year two and is already being talked about as one of the game's top linebackers. Schwesinger plays with sideline-to-sideline speed and a nose for the football. He is the kind of player who thrives in an attacking defense. And that is what Rutenberg wants. Even without Garrett, this scheme will be aggressive. It will blitz. It will stunt. It will create confusion. The question is whether it can create consistent pressure. Because in the modern NFL, if you cannot get home with four-man rushes, quarterbacks will shred you. Patrick Mahomes, Josh Allen, Lamar Jackson. These guys eat up soft pressure. You need to make them uncomfortable. And I am not sure this defensive line, even with Verse, can do that consistently yet.
card_lines: Can they get home without Garrett?

paragraphs.text: Let me give you one more historical parallel. The two thousand Baltimore Ravens defense. In two thousand, the Ravens won the Super Bowl with one of the greatest defenses ever. They had Ray Lewis, Rod Woodson, and a ferocious pass rush. But that defense was not built on one player. It was built on depth, scheme, and attitude. Eleven guys who believed they were the baddest unit on the planet. That is what the Browns need to become. They cannot out-talent teams with Garrett gone. So they need to out-hit them. Out-hustle them. Out-scheme them. That is the only way this works. And if it does work, this could actually be a defining moment for this franchise. Not the end of an era. But the beginning of a new one. A defense that wins with collective toughness instead of individual brilliance.
card_lines: Not built on 1 star, built on depth & attitude

sections.heading: Training Camp Battles and the Road Ahead

paragraphs.text: Here is what we are seeing in training camp right now. Day twelve just wrapped, and head coach Todd Monken is not happy with pre-snap penalties. He reportedly threw his headset during practice and then apologized to the room afterward. That is a sixty-year-old first-year head coach trying to install discipline. It is also a sign that this team is still figuring out its identity under new leadership. Monken replaced Kevin Stefanski, who was fired after six seasons. Stefanski is now in Atlanta, by the way, and he is running live tackling periods in Falcons camp, something they never did under his predecessor. Meanwhile, Monken is in Cleveland dealing with false starts and delay-of-game penalties. Same flags. Different coach. That has to change.
card_lines: Stefanski fired after 6 years, now in ATL
Same flags, different coach = must change

paragraphs.text: On the defensive side, one of the big camp storylines is Mason Graham. He is the defensive tackle taken in the first round of the twenty twenty-six draft out of Michigan. Graham is expected to anchor the interior alongside Maliek Collins. But Graham missed practice on day twelve with an undisclosed injury, and that is a concern. The Browns lack depth on the defensive line. If Graham or Collins go down for any extended period, this defense is in serious trouble. Mike Hall Junior is the primary backup, but he has struggled to stay healthy. Kalia Davis and Adin Huntington are also in the mix, but neither is a proven starter. Depth is a real issue here. And that is magnified when you no longer have a player like Myles Garrett who can single-handedly wreck a game.

The Browns also made some roster moves this week. They claimed defensive lineman Coziah Izzard off waivers after another D-lineman, Sam Kamara, left practice early with an injury. They also added cornerback Tyler Hall, who most recently played for Seattle. These are depth moves, but they tell you the coaching staff is worried about attrition. Eleven players missed the second day of full pads, according to ESPN. That is a lot of bodies on the sideline in early August. And when you are trying to install a new scheme and build a new defensive identity, you need reps. You need continuity. Injuries disrupt that. So the health of this roster over the next three weeks will be absolutely critical as they prepare for the preseason opener against Chicago.
card_lines: Claimed DL Coziah Izzard off waivers
Added CB Tyler Hall from Seahawks
11 players missed Day 2 of full pads

paragraphs.text: Let me address the elephant in the room. The quarterback situation. Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders are battling for the starting job, and the Browns have listed them as co-starters on the depth chart. Watson has struggled in camp. Another interception on day twelve. Sanders has been more consistent, completing twenty-one of twenty-five passes in one practice. But here is the thing. It does not matter who wins the quarterback job if this defense cannot hold up. The Browns are not going to outscore teams this year. They do not have the offensive firepower. Their path to winning is the same as it has always been. Run the football. Control the clock. Play elite defense. And if that third element falls apart without Myles Garrett, this season is going to be ugly no matter who is under center.
paragraphs.card_title: QB Battle and the Bigger Picture
card_lines: Watson vs Sanders: co-starters on depth chart
Formula: run ball, control clock, elite D

paragraphs.text: So where does that leave us? The Cleveland Browns are at a crossroads. They traded away the best defensive player in franchise history. They hired a new head coach and a new defensive coordinator. They rebuilt the offensive line. They are navigating a quarterback competition. There is so much change happening at once. And in the middle of all that chaos, they need to prove that their defense can still be elite. Not because of one superstar. But because of a collective identity. Because of scheme. Because of attitude. That is what we are watching for in training camp. Can Jared Verse become a consistent edge threat? Can Isaiah McGuire take the next step? Can the secondary carry this defense while the pass rush develops? Those are the questions that will define the twenty twenty-six season.
card_lines: New HC, new DC, rebuilt O-line, QB battle
Can defense be elite without 1 superstar?

paragraphs.text: I will leave you with this. The Browns do not play their preseason opener until this Saturday against the Bears. That game will give us our first real look at what this defense can do. Who gets reps with the ones. How the pass rush rotation shakes out. Whether the secondary can make plays. But the real test comes in Week One of the regular season. That is when the bullets are live. That is when offensive coordinators game-plan specifically to attack your weaknesses. And without Myles Garrett, this defense has weaknesses it has not had in nine years. Can they overcome them? We are about to find out. This is the post-Garrett era in Cleveland. And the identity of this franchise hangs in the balance.
card_lines: Post-Garrett era: franchise identity at stake

sections.heading: What History Teaches Us About Life After a Legend

paragraphs.text: Let me give you some perspective. When great players leave, teams panic. They try to replace the irreplaceable. But the smartest franchises do not try to find the next version of that player. They reinvent themselves. Look at the San Francisco Forty-Niners after Joe Montana left. They did not try to find another Montana. They built a different offense around Steve Young. Same system. Different strengths. Or look at the New England Patriots after Tom Brady. They did not try to draft another Brady. They accepted that era was over and started fresh. The Browns need to do the same thing. Myles Garrett is gone. Accept it. Move on. Build a defense that does not rely on one player doing superhuman things every Sunday. Build a defense that wins with depth, discipline, and execution. That is how you survive losing a legend.
card_lines: 49ers after Montana: built around Young differently
Pats after Brady: started fresh, didn't replace

paragraphs.text: And here is the thing. Jared Verse is not a bad consolation prize. He is twenty-four years old. He has already made two Pro Bowls. He has averaged six sacks per season in his first two years. If he can push that number to eight or nine sacks in year three, and if Isaiah McGuire can give you six or seven, and if Alex Wright can give you five, suddenly you have an eighteen to twenty-sack rotation from your edge rushers. That is not Myles Garrett territory. But it is enough to be competitive. Add in Mason Graham and Maliek Collins generating interior pressure, and you can manufacture a pass rush. It will not be dominant. But it can be good enough. Especially if the secondary is as good as advertised and Carson Schwesinger continues to develop into a star linebacker.
card_lines: Verse: 24 years old, 2x Pro Bowl, 6 sacks/year avg
Add Graham/Collins interior = viable pass rush

paragraphs.text: The wild card is Mike Rutenberg's scheme. He kept the attacking foundation from Jim Schwartz, but he is adding disguise and exotic looks. Grant Delpit said there is a lot of communication required in this defense. That means pre-snap movement. That means confusion for quarterbacks. That means zone blitzes and simulated pressures. If Rutenberg can make opposing offenses guess, if he can create hesitation in the pocket, that buys his pass rushers an extra half-second. And in the NFL, a half-second is the difference between a sack and a completion. So the scheme matters. It is not just about talent. It is about putting your players in position to succeed. And if Rutenberg can do that, this defense might surprise people. It might not be the juggernaut it was with Garrett. But it can still be a top-ten unit.

But let me be honest with you. I am skeptical. I have watched too many teams lose a Hall of Fame player and spiral. The Indianapolis Colts after Peyton Manning. The Green Bay Packers in the transition from Brett Favre to Aaron Rodgers. The Detroit Lions after Calvin Johnson retired. Losing generational talent changes everything. And the Browns are not just losing Garrett. They are also dealing with a new head coach, a quarterback controversy, and an offensive line that features five potential new starters. That is a lot of variables. And when you have that many unknowns, things can go sideways fast. So yes, I hope this defense proves me wrong. I hope Jared Verse becomes a star. I hope Isaiah McGuire breaks out. But hope is not a strategy. And right now, the Browns are hoping a lot of things break right.
card_lines: History: teams spiral after losing HOF talent
Browns: new HC, QB battle, O-line rebuild too

paragraphs.text: Here is what I will be watching as camp continues. First, Isaiah McGuire's development. If he can consistently win one-on-one matchups, that changes everything. Second, Mason Graham's health. If he misses significant time, this defensive line is in serious trouble. Third, the secondary's ability to create turnovers. Grant Delpit already has three interceptions in camp. Can he maintain that ball production? Fourth, Carson Schwesinger's progression. If he takes another leap forward, he can be the defensive leader this team needs without Garrett. And fifth, the overall attitude of this defense. Do they have a chip on their shoulder? Are they playing angry? Because talent alone will not get it done. They need to play with an edge. They need to prove the doubters wrong. Starting with me.
card_lines: 5. Attitude: chip on shoulder, edge, anger

paragraphs.text: So that is where we stand on August twelfth, twenty twenty-six. The Browns are deep into training camp. The defense is trying to reinvent itself without Myles Garrett. The offensive line is a work in progress. The quarterback battle is unresolved. And the season is just weeks away. This is not the ideal scenario. But it is the reality. And the only way forward is to embrace it. Stop looking back at what Myles Garrett used to do. Start focusing on what Jared Verse, Isaiah McGuire, and this entire defense can become. Because if they can build a collective identity, if they can play with attitude and discipline, if they can prove that this team is more than one man, then maybe, just maybe, this defense can still be elite. That is the challenge. That is the opportunity. And over the next few weeks, we will find out if they are up to it.
card_lines: Stop looking back at Garrett era
Focus on what Verse/McGuire can become
Challenge & opportunity: prove elite without star
